title: The office crisis
dek: Hybrid work gutted office values while refinancing walls and conversion pipelines reshape American cities.
one_sentence: Office vacancy broke the revenue model for real estate and architecture, forcing a decade-long reckoning on distressed towers and refinance cliffs.
lede: The office sector is in structural crisis. National office vacancy peaked at 19.6% in Q1 2025 and only fell to 17.7% by mid-2026 — a level that economists call unrecoverable. Hybrid work broke the occupancy math. Higher interest rates broke the refinance math. Both forces hit at once, and the collision reshaped the entire commercial real estate sector.
what_changed:
Hybrid work gutted office occupancy. When employees stopped coming in five days a week, vacancy exploded across secondary and tertiary markets. San Francisco and Austin — both tech hubs — saw vacancy rates exceed 26% by 2025. Class B and C office buildings became economically obsolete overnight. The only offices that stayed strong were Class A trophy assets in central business districts, the kind that multinational firms anchor with prestigious leases. Every other building — the mid-market office, the suburban corporate park, the regional tower — faced a choice: find new tenants who no longer existed, or die.

The refinance crisis turned distress into catastrophe. In commercial real estate, assets mature on predictable cycles: a loan taken out in 2013 comes due in 2023 or 2024. In 2025 alone, $957 billion in CRE loans matured. Through 2028, another $2.8 trillion comes due. Lenders who refinanced at 3% rates can now only get 6% or 7%. The math breaks. If occupancy is down 20 percent and rents are flat, the owner cannot service new debt at double the cost. CMBS delinquencies reached 7.29% in 2025 — the highest distress signal in the market. Chapter 11 bankruptcies hit a 10-year high, with 694 corporate filings in 2025, the most in 14 years.

Conversion became the survival strategy. Instead of fighting for tenants, real estate owners pivoted to adaptive reuse: tearing out office cubicles and building apartments. Office-to-apartment conversions reached 90,300 units in 2026, a 28% jump year-over-year. Now 47 percent of the entire 193,900-unit adaptive reuse pipeline is former office space. This signals defeat. It means owners acknowledged that the office market will not recover at historical occupancy rates. It means they see more value in apartments — a bet on the housing shortage (3.4 million homes short nationally) and the 105 percent premium to buy versus rent — than in rehabilitating their office towers.

Architecture felt the shockwave first and hardest. When office construction cratered, billings collapsed. The Architecture Billings Index hit 47.6 in October 2025, a reading below 50 that signals declining demand. Thirty-eight percent of firms reported falling revenue. Small independent practices, already thin on margins, took the biggest hit: firms with under $250,000 in annual billings expected a 7 percent revenue drop. Seventy percent of declining firms cited fewer new projects ahead. AI software accelerated the squeeze, automating site planning, specification writing, code-violation detection, and BIM workflows. Larger, consolidated firms integrated these tools fast; smaller practices could not compete and faced pressure to merge or shut down. Meanwhile, consolidators like Stantec acquired UK firm Hydrock in May 2024, adding 950 professionals and signaling that private equity saw opportunity in rolled-up, consolidated practices. The sector is consolidating under pressure, not from growth, but from survival.

win: Real estate investment trusts and large, consolidated architecture and engineering firms are riding the conversion wave. Industrial real estate thrives: 940 million sq ft leased in 2025, the second-best year on record, as e-commerce tenants account for 56% of retail goods sales growth. Large consolidated practices — especially those backed by PE capital — integrate AI tools, absorb smaller competitors, and win the shrinking pool of projects. Only Class A trophy offices in CBDs retain premium occupancy; owners there hold pricing power.
lose: Mid-market and Class B/C office owners face decade-long losses and forced debt restructuring. Small independent architecture practices are squeezed hardest: facing revenue declines of 7 percent, unable to afford AI tools, and losing deals to consolidated competitors. Junior architects and traditional drafting roles face automation. Real estate development firms focused on office are obsolete or in bankruptcy. worry: The biggest risk is a cascading debt spiral. CMBS delinquencies are already at 7.29%, but the real wave hits 2027-2028 when the bulk of the $2.8 trillion refinance wall matures. Owners who cannot reposition (convert, or sell at a loss) will default, flooding the market with distressed assets and depressing pricing further. A debt standstill among major commercial landlords could choke both capital availability and development momentum for years. If conversion pipelines saturate and apartment supply finally catches up to demand, the single remaining exit for office owners closes, and a permanent loss spiral begins.

title: Adaptive Reuse & Conversion
dek: Dead offices get gutted and rebuilt—but the contractors doing it are starving on thin margins.
lede: Hybrid work killed the demand for traditional office space. Rates stayed high. So millions of square feet of Class-B and Class-C office buildings now sit half-empty, especially in secondary markets. That creates a real opportunity: tear out the cubicles, rewire for apartments or mixed-use, and sell the landlord a comeback story. But the contractors doing that work are trapped between material inflation, tariff shock, and a grinding shortage of skilled workers—all crushing margins that were already razor-thin.
what_changed:
Hybrid work erased 41% of demand for office space since 2019. New office deliveries fell 26% in 2025 alone. National office vacancy sits at 17.6% (April 2026), but the real problem is concentrated: Miami's at 12.5%, but Seattle's bleeding at 25.2%. Class-A trophy towers still command premiums and find tenants; it's the older Class-B and Class-C buildings—the bread-and-butter stock in every American city—that are now dead weight. Those buildings can't compete on price because their rents don't cover debt service at 5.7–6.6% mortgage rates. The math just doesn't work. So owners are forced to either sell at a loss or convert.

That conversion is real work, and it's real opportunity. An office building can become apartments, hotels, co-working, light industrial, storage, mixed-use retail-and-housing. The Commercial Property Remodeling market is $39.8 billion (2026), up from $45.2 billion in 2022 in dollar terms—but that's nominal inflation, not growth. The CAGR from 2021 to 2026 is just 0.8%. In 2026 alone, the market grew only 1.5%. Meanwhile, material costs surged 40.3% from January 2021 to April 2026. Tariffs added another layer: 50% on steel and aluminum, 15% on industrial equipment, 10% on softwood lumber. Contractors are reporting total project escalation of 6–10% just from tariff stacks. That eats the margin. Contractors were already squeezing 3.6% margins (2022), and those are probably compressed further by 2026 due to tariffs and labor inflation.

Labor is the second guillotine. Commercial building construction has a 500,000-worker shortage that costs the industry $10.8 billion annually. The shortage is structural: retirements and chronic underinvestment in trades training mean there simply aren't enough HVAC techs, electricians, plumbers, and framers to go around. Wages are climbing faster than inflation itself—residential construction wages jumped 9.2% year-over-year in mid-2025. Contractors can't turn to offshore labor or automation for the craft work involved in adaptive reuse; every old building is different. They either hire at inflated wages or they turn away jobs. For mid-market remodeling, many are turning away jobs.

But there's an undertow of consolidation happening. Commercial HVAC and mechanical trades are being rolled up by private equity—Blackstone/Legence, Morgan Stanley/Sila, Leonard Green/Wrench—and subcontractor acquisition volume jumped 38.6% year-over-year to 366 deals in 2025. The theory is that larger platforms can absorb tariff inflation through volume, leverage supply chains better, and lock in labor by offering better benefits. Meanwhile, commercial chapter 11 filings hit a 10-year high in 2025 and surged another 76% year-over-year in January 2026 versus January 2025. With $875 billion in commercial mortgages maturing in 2026, refinancing is a bloodbath for anybody who overlevered into office.

If tariffs stay at 50% on steel through 2026–2027, and construction wages keep climbing at 9%+ annually, the math breaks. Owners might simply hold empty buildings and wait for a recession or tariff relief rather than convert. title: The Housing Squeeze
dek: High rates freeze buying and pressure multifamily even as housing stays scarce.
lede: The housing market faces a squeeze from two sides at once. Buyers can't afford to buy because rates stay near 6%, while landlords in rent-controlled cities can't raise rents fast enough to cover soaring insurance and labor costs. The result: a frozen market where builders cut prices and offer mortgage buydowns, apartment companies merge into mega-REITs to survive, and smaller operators face bankruptcy.
what_changed:
Higher interest rates broke the math on both sides of the housing market. On the homebuilding side, a buyer who could afford a $400,000 house with a 3% rate now can't afford that same house at 6%. Builders saw housing starts crash 15.4% from January to May 2026, hitting 1.177 million units—the lowest since May 2020. Rather than wait for demand to return, they've started cutting prices by an average of 5% and offering to pay down mortgage rates for buyers just to move inventory. At the same time, construction tariffs hit 25-30% in 2025, raising the cost of each home by about $10,900, and labor shortages cost the industry $10.8 billion annually. Builders are getting caught between higher input costs and lower prices—a squeeze that squeezes margins from 6.1% in 2022 down to 6-8% by 2026. In response, the industry is consolidating fast. Between August 2025 and June 2026, the share of builders reporting acquisition approaches doubled from 9% to 18%, and major deals like Taylor Morrison going to Berkshire Hathaway, Tri Pointe to Sumitomo Forestry, and United Homes Group to Stanley Martin show that only scale survives. The US home builders industry is now flat at $166.2 billion in 2026 revenue with near-zero growth, a far cry from the building boom of 2021–2023.

On the rental side, the squeeze takes a different form. After years of climbing rents—double-digit growth in 2021–2023—the apartment market hit a wall. Vacancy rates climbed from 6.3% in 2021 to 7.0% in Q2 2025, and luxury segments sit at 11.4% vacant. Developers chased the rent-growth tailwind and built aggressively in the Sun Belt and Mountain West, but when occupancy tightened, owners stopped raising rents and started offering concessions instead. The apartment rental market is still huge at $305.7 billion in 2026 revenue, but growth has slowed to 1.7% annually. Worse, rent-controlled markets like New York and California face a cruel squeeze. Tenants pay record-high percentages of their income for housing, yet landlords cannot raise rents fast enough—NYC caps increases at 2.75%–5.25% per year, California at 5% plus inflation capped at 10%—to cover surging insurance, labor, and maintenance costs. Multifamily loan delinquencies hit 1.37% in Q3 2025, a 3.4× increase over two years and the highest since 2008. Smaller leveraged owners and rent-stabilized properties face the worst of it: Pinnacle filed for bankruptcy in May 2025 with $500M in mortgage debt; 5,100 of its rent-stabilized NYC apartments went to auction. Sonder, the short-term rental company, collapsed entirely when Marriott terminated its licensing deal and it filed for Chapter 7 liquidation in 2025. Consolidation is the only exit. AvalonBay Communities and Equity Residential announced a $69 billion merger to create the nation's largest apartment REIT with 180,000+ units and $175M in cost cuts expected within 18 months—a vote of no confidence in independent operators' ability to survive.

What became scarce? Affordable housing, paradoxically, even though oversupply is pushing rents down in competitive markets. In rent-controlled cities, supply is locked in place by regulation, and demand for those cheap units far exceeds supply. What became cheap? Single-family homes, at least in hot markets like Florida and Texas where builders are cutting prices to clear inventory. What became risky? Leverage on apartment buildings, especially those with rent-stabilized portfolios that can't cover rising costs. What became newly valuable? Scale and capital strength. Big builders like D.R. Horton and Lennar can absorb tariff shocks and rate headwinds; small builders get acquired or disappear. Big REITs like the new AvalonBay-Equity Residential colossus can negotiate better insurance rates, automate labor, and hide losses in diversified portfolios; small mom-and-pop landlords go bankrupt.

A cascading default scenario could freeze credit and tip the broader economy into recession.

title: Logistics & Data Centers: Capital Finds Electricity
dek: Warehouses and data centers pull capital from office towers because they move goods and compute, not people—and the race for power has reshaped what matters most.
lede: Hybrid work killed the case for downtown office towers. But it also turned AI and e-commerce from trends into infrastructure problems. Developers and capital are no longer fighting over square footage. They're fighting over power, grid access, and the industrial real estate that can handle 30-100 kW per rack or move packages at scale. The U.S. colocation market has nearly doubled in five years—from $26 billion in 2021 to $72 billion in 2026—and that money is still moving.
what_changed:
For fifteen years, colocation facilities were cheap and plentiful. A data center operator could lease space, plug in servers, and compete on price. That game is over. AI training demands 30 to 100 kilowatts per single server rack. Inference at 10 to 20 kW per rack still looks simple until you multiply by thousands. The constraint flipped: electricity is now the scarcity, not space. North American colocation occupancy hit 1% vacancy in 2026. Operators are buying sites not for acreage but for power—proximity to hydroelectric dams, natural gas plants, or utilities willing to guarantee grid capacity. The Texas hyperscale campus that ECP and KKR announced in July 2025 (part of a $50 billion AI infrastructure partnership) exists because Texas utilities have capacity. The U.K. subsidiary acquisition by Digital Realty ($200 million, July 2024) happened because London has grid slots.

The electrical grid itself became the bottleneck. Grid interconnection requests now exceed 1,400 GW stuck in queue, with lead times of four to five years for high-capacity connections in saturated markets like Northern Virginia, Dallas, and Phoenix. In December 2025, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) broke the dam by issuing data-center-specific transmission tariffs for the PJM Interconnection—the largest regional grid operator. Starting January 2026, data centers had to follow new rules about how they buy power and pay for grid upgrades. Oregon's POWER Act (August 2025) flipped the model: facilities over 20 MW now must sign ten-year power-purchase agreements with renewable generators. California and Virginia followed with large-load tariffs starting at 25-40 MW thresholds. Power pricing jumped 17-19% in the last two years—the first sustained spike after fifteen years of decline.

Capital is flowing to the operators and utilities that control power, not space. Equinix and Digital Realty—the two largest U.S. colocation companies (10.28% and 9.98% market share in 2024)—are consolidating smaller operators and bidding aggressively on grid contracts. The market is growing at 11.5% compound annual growth in the U.S. through 2030, and globally at 14% CAGR, but that growth is narrowing to companies with utility partnerships, real estate in high-power zones, and access to capital to build custom cooling (liquid-cooled racks need specialized design).

Meanwhile, logistics real estate is less dramatic but just as locked in. Warehouses that move boxes—parcel hubs, last-mile centers, regional distribution nodes—have become essential to the e-commerce flywheel. That demand is steady and boring, which is exactly why capital moved there. Unlike offices (uncertain occupancy) or data centers (capital-intensive, technically risky), logistics is a proven yield play: ground leases at 6-8% on income-producing assets in tier-1 nodes (Atlanta, Dallas, Los Angeles, Chicago). The rents on well-located warehouses have held firm even as office space craters, because the goods still have to move.

Regulatory shift: Oregon POWER Act (August 2025), California and Virginia large-load tariffs (2025-2026), and FY 2026 federal infrastructure authorization cliff (September 2026) reshaping regional competitiveness.
win: Operators with power contracts win—Equinix and Digital Realty (10.28% and 9.98% U.S. market share) consolidate smaller rivals and ink utility deals. Regions with stable renewable power or utility capacity (Texas, Oregon, parts of the Pacific Northwest) attract the bulk of new hyperscale investment. Logistics operators in tier-1 nodes see steady demand and pricing power because goods still need to move, and e-commerce growth is inelastic to recessions. States and utilities that act fast on power policy—Oregon's fast-track PPAs, FERC's new tariffs—become migration magnets for AI infrastructure capex that used to flow to office parks.
lose: Developers who own empty office towers get squeezed as capital rotates to power-constrained data centers and logistics hubs. Mid-market colocation operators without utility partnerships face margin collapse as power costs rise 17-19% and occupancy is already maxed. Construction firms building data center campuses face labor shortages and tariffs on materials—heavy engineering construction margins are compressing from 7.5% to 5% even as labor wages jump 8-12% annually. States without power capacity or outdated grid infrastructure lose AI capex entirely; Northern Virginia is saturated, and grid queues now favor greenfield sites in deregulated regions.
worry: The power grid itself is the single biggest fragility. Interconnection queues exceed 1,400 GW with four-to-five-year waits for new capacity in saturated markets. If AI demand keeps accelerating and utilities can't build capacity fast enough, data center operators will face forced load-shedding, outages, or have to build their own on-site generation (hugely expensive and regionally constrained by fuel supply and environmental permitting). A hard recession could stall the federal infrastructure funding that has propped up heavy construction, since authorization expires in September 2026 and state/local budgets are already tight. If grid tariffs or renewable PPAs become unaffordable, AI capex could freeze or migrate offshore to cheaper electricity zones, leaving U.S. colocation operators with expensive build-outs and no demand.
one_sentence: Capital flowed from office real estate to logistics and data centers because they move goods and compute—but now the constraint is electricity, not space, and power access has become the only moat that matters.

title: Owning the Land
dek: Land leasing and RV parks shift from growth to scarcity—a steady, consolidating landlord business serving renters priced out of home ownership.
one_sentence: As office towers empty and traditional housing becomes unaffordable, capital quietly rotates into land leasing, RV parks, and manufactured housing—where occupancy stays near 95% and pricing power grows because supply is stuck.
lede: Office real estate lost its tenant base to hybrid work and rising interest rates killed its financing math. But capital doesn't disappear—it rotates. Into land. Into RV parks. Into manufactured housing communities. These asset classes are small, sleepy-sounding, and boring by design. They're also consolidating fast, commanding near-total occupancy, and printing 47% margins while traditional property chokes.
what_changed:
Land leasing in the US is a $16.0 billion market (2026) moving at 0.6% CAGR since 2022, but growth is accelerating right now because housing is genuinely unaffordable. The industry serves two overlapping populations squeezed out of homeownership: price-conscious renters who can't afford stick-built homes, and retirees who are aging through their 60s and 70s and don't want property maintenance. RV adoption stayed high after the pandemic as remote work made mobility realistic. Occupancy rates sit near 95%—nearly full—and land leasing operators pushed through 7% rent growth in 2025 without backing down. That pricing power comes from scarcity. New community development is stuck. Zoning boards in most states treat manufactured housing as a nuisance, forcing developers to spend 24-48 months and $60,000 per site just to get a new campground or mobile home community open. Each year the supply stays constrained, existing operators become harder to dislodge.

Regulators are starting to notice the rental squeeze and pushing back: Washington state capped annual lot rent increases at 5% in May 2025, and Florida and Virginia are loosening zoning to allow more manufactured homes. But these policy moves won't matter if supply stays locked. In campgrounds and RV parks—a subset of land leasing that's $11.3 billion and flat to declining in volume—the structural play is even clearer. Total reservations fell 1.0% in 2025, the first annual decline in platform history, but revenue rose 5.2%. Operators raised prices instead of filling more sites. Average nightly rates at medium parks jumped 16.6% to $83. This is the opposite of growth-through-expansion; it's yield-through-power. Glamping—luxury camping with comfortable beds and hot showers—grew 43.6% while regular RV parks flatlined, revealing that younger, remote workers are willing to pay premium prices for a mobile lifestyle. Consolidation is accelerating. Sun Communities spent $457 million in October 2025 acquiring 14 manufactured housing and RV communities, then immediately divested its 129-property marina portfolio to exit a riskier business. KOA added new communities in North Carolina and Massachusetts in 2025, but these are rare; most capital is flowing into consolidation of existing sites, not greenfield development.

The economics are becoming clearer too. Cap rates for institutional investors sit at 8.0%, but the actual cost of borrowing runs 8.7-9.3% per year. That means day-one leverage is negative; returns depend on slowly paying down debt and repositioning the asset, not on cash-on-cash returns. This is not a get-rich-quick play. It's a bond-substitute play: you're taking operational leverage and accepting single-digit cash flow yields in exchange for inflation-protected rent growth and full occupancy. The 47.3% EBIT margins for land leasing (2026) are remarkably stable because the operator is just charging rent and maintaining infrastructure; there's no variable cost to scale. Labor is rising—parks struggle to hire groundskeeping staff—but that's a cost of maintaining the asset, not a margin killer. The 2025 Guadalupe River flood and Hurricane Helene exposed uninsured waterfront risk and prompted Texas to tighten safety codes, but this just favors larger REITs who can absorb insurance costs and regulatory adaptation. There are ~98,000 land leasing operators in the US (2026), ranging from one-person lot rentals to huge REITs like ELS (452 communities, 173,201 sites) and Sun Communities (5,000+ communities). Consolidation is accelerating because small operators can't navigate zoning friction, insurance risk, and regulatory patchwork anymore.

title: Hotels as Real Estate
dek: The lodging market bifurcates into high-margin luxury and extended-stay while economy motels collapse as chains financialize the category as an asset class.
lede: The US hotel industry is stuck. Market size inched from $258.1 billion in 2022 to $286.5 billion in 2025, but that 0.5% growth masks a story of radical bifurcation: luxury boutiques pulled 6% revenue gains while economy properties contracted, extended-stay hotels captured supply growth, and Sonder's November 2025 bankruptcy shocked the market. Higher rates broke the capital math for conversion plays and independent operators, and labor scarcity made skeleton crews the new normal.
what_changed:
Higher interest rates killed the conversion-play economics that had kept the hotel pipeline full. For years, investors could acquire distressed motels, pour capex into a refresh, and refinance at a spread over treasuries. By 2025, that math inverted: debt service on empty properties became toxic, maturity walls hit Q4 2025 through Q1 2026, and Revo Hospitality Group's 260 properties landed in Chapter 11. Sonder, the Marriott-backed boutique tech startup, collapsed in November 2025 after the licensing deal severed, stranded guests mid-stay, and left its asset base in limbo. The refinancing crisis was real: hotels that could not roll over loans were forced to sell, compress capex, or file for restructuring.

Simultaneously, the labor cost wall inverted the margin ladder. Wages for hotel staff rose 25.6% versus 2019, and labor cost per occupied room jumped 21% from Q4 2024 to Q4 2025, hitting $54.98 by year-end. Operating costs exploded too: insurance premiums up 100%, utilities up 30% from 2024 to 2025, while demand flatlined after the pandemic recovery bounce. Large chains could absorb these hits by running skeleton crews with 70-80% annual turnover and automating guest-facing functions. Independent operators and smaller chains could not. By 2026, boutique hotels with tighter unit economics faced compression of average margins from 18.4% in 2016 down to 15.1% in 2026, making refinancing harder and forcing consolidation.

What made lodging newly valuable was scale and distribution, not the property itself. Luxury boutique hotels achieved average daily rates of $452 in 2025 with RevPAR of $307, well above the industry-wide luxury average of $263, because they could command premium pricing from high-frequency travelers and corporate accounts. Extended-stay hotels grew supply by 4% in 2025, the largest increase in four years, occupying 12.4% above industry-average occupancy because they served project-based employment and hybrid work relocations, not one-off travelers. Casino hotels bifurcated by destination: premium Las Vegas resorts remained resilient with higher-value customers per room, while mid-tier regional casinos faced slower traffic and price competition, reflecting geographic pricing power. What made rooms cheap was economy lodging: traditional midscale and budget properties faced contraction because their occupancy could not sustain their debt loads at 2025 borrowing costs.

The real money rotated to asset financialization. IHG opened a record 443 hotels in Q1 2026, passing 7,000 operating hotels with 1.03 million rooms, and signed 694 additional properties, converting franchising into a real-estate brokerage. Hyatt acquired Playa Hotels & Resorts for $2.6 billion in 2025, and Blackstone purchased Hamilton Island for $1.2 billion, treating resort properties as collateral-backed income streams rather than hospitality operations. Fertitta Entertainment offered $7 billion for Caesars Entertainment (a $31.5 billion deal including debt) expected to close late 2026 or early 2027, consolidating casino properties into a mega-operator with 60 casinos. VICI Properties acquired Golden Portfolio properties (7 casinos) in April 2026 for $1.15 billion and Gamehost assets in Canada for $141 million in June 2026, positioning itself as a landlord to casino operators rather than an operator itself. Hilton launched its Outset Collection with 60+ properties in pipeline, targeting independent owners seeking global distribution without losing brand autonomy. In essence, the property became the collateral, the franchise became the moat, and the occupancy rate became the bond yield.

Economy and traditional midscale properties contracted throughout 2025 because their occupancy could not justify their debt service at higher rates and their labor costs could not be absorbed by lower RevPAR. Mid-tier regional casinos lost pricing power and foot traffic, forced to compete on discounts rather than experience. Guests in stranded Sonder locations lost access mid-stay. Workers in hospitality faced the highest wage gains (25.6% since 2019) but also the highest turnover (70-80% annually), suggesting jobs became temporary and unstable despite raises.

Regional casinos face regulatory fragmentation: Illinois, Indiana, Hawaii, Maine, and others are legalizing online casinos and micro-betting, which will siphon players from land-based resorts and require operators to choose between maintaining price and defending volume. If online expansion accelerates, mid-tier regional casinos could face a 10-15% revenue loss within three years, triggering another wave of bankruptcies and asset fire-sales.

title: Retail's Property Fallout
dek: Store closures are flooding retail real estate onto the market as tariffs and e-commerce crush the department store model.
lede: Department stores, the backbone of American shopping malls for decades, are imploding. Tariff rates jumped from 14.7% in January 2025 to 35.1% by December 2025, crushing margins. Saks Global—which had just merged Saks Fifth Avenue, Neiman Marcus, and Bergdorf Goodman—filed for bankruptcy in January 2026 carrying $3.4 billion in debt. Macy's is closing 150 stores by end-2026, dumping prime retail real estate onto the market faster than it can be repurposed.
what_changed:
For decades, a department store on Main Street or in a regional mall was money: stable anchor tenant, foot traffic, reliable credit quality. That math broke in 2025-2026. Tariffs on apparel imports exploded—14.7% in January 2025, climbing to 35.1% by December 2025—compressing margins industry-wide from 6.1% in 2024 to an estimated 3.6% if retailers absorbed the costs. Retailers had three bad choices: eat the tariff hit and wipe out profit, pass it to customers and watch traffic tank, or manufacture differently. None worked. Saks Global, carrying $3.4 billion in debt after its December 2024 merger of three iconic luxury banners, hit a wall in January 2026 when vendor payment delays cascaded and store productivity collapsed. That bankruptcy was the signal. It told landlords that even prestige retail was vulnerable.

Mainstream department stores followed. Macy's executed a controlled retreat, closing 50 stores by end-2024, then 66 in 2025, with 14 more planned for 2026—that's 150 doors gone, each one freeing a landlord to either hold vacant space, discount massively, or let the tenant walk. JCPenney's FY2024 revenue fell to $6.6 billion despite a 'Yes, JCPenney' comeback campaign that lifted May 2025 traffic by 3%. Nordstrom's family launched a $3.8 billion bid to take the company private in late 2025-2026, signaling they saw more value in the off-price Rack format than in traditional department stores. The shift was structural, not cyclical. Consumer spending bifurcated: affluent households kept spending; lower and middle-income households traded down to discount stores at five times faster rates in 2026, with inflation (PCE up 4.1% year-over-year as of May 2026) driving the wedge. Discount stores and off-price retailers (TJX, Ross) won that migration. Department stores were caught in the middle, losing traffic to cheaper channels above and below them.

The real estate consequence is cascading vacancy and repricing. Mall anchors are no longer anchors. Department store real estate—prime 50,000-100,000-square-foot boxes in regional malls and downtowns—is flooding the market with no clear next tenant. The 666,500 employees in US department stores are declining 2.87% annually through 2028; fewer jobs means weaker demand for nearby service space, parking, and logistics. Landlords face a choice: hold space at distressed rents, convert to fitness, dining, or entertainment, or accept lease terminations and redevelop. Each option destroys value vs. the pre-2020 model. Off-price and discount retail are expanding—Ross Stores reported comparable store sales up 17% in Q3 2025 and announced ~110 new store openings for 2026—but those boxes are smaller, lower-rent, and serve different locations. They won't fill the real estate vacuum left by department store collapse.

TJX and other value formats are capturing traffic from the collapsing mid-tier. The "treasure hunt" experience of curated, changing inventory remains defensible against e-commerce, so discount stores are outperforming traditional department stores across the board. Nordstrom's family, betting $3.8 billion on taking the company private, sees the future in Rack expansion, not in full-line department stores. Logistics and alternative uses for vacated real estate may also win—repurposed department store boxes can become storage, fitness, dining, or entertainment venues if landlords are creative.
lose: Department store landlords and the vendors, workers, and service providers that depend on them are getting squeezed. Macy's is closing 150 stores by end-2026; JCPenney is fighting for survival despite a 3% traffic bump; even luxury collapsed (Saks Global bankruptcy). Department store employees are declining 2.87% annually through 2028. Mall owners are losing their anchor tenants. Landlords are either holding vacant space, offering fire-sale rents to attract new tenants (who may never come), or accepting lease terminations and redevelopment losses. Regional malls that built their entire model around department store anchors are facing existential questions about their future.
worry: The biggest risk is the speed and cascade of store closures creating a real estate death spiral in regional malls and secondary downtowns. Macy's 150 stores, Saks Global bankruptcy, JCPenney's struggles, and smaller retailers' exits are all happening in 2025-2026 simultaneously. As landlords lose anchor tenants and traffic, they cut maintenance, raise rents on remaining tenants (squeezing smaller shops), and the mall spirals down. Secondary and tertiary locations are most vulnerable—a mall in a smaller metro loses its Macy's and has no clear alternative anchor. If landlords can't find new uses or tenants fast enough, you see vacancy cascades, property value crashes, and forced sales at steep discounts that ripple through REIT portfolios and commercial property financing.

title: The commercial-debt wall
dek: When $2.8 trillion in maturing loans hit refinancing at higher rates, the math breaks.
one_sentence: Commercial real estate borrowers are staring down a refinancing crisis: nearly $1 trillion in loans came due in 2025 alone, and $2.8 trillion more mature through 2028, all refinancing at rates 190 basis points higher than their originals.
lede: The commercial real estate sector is running into a wall. Not the office crisis, though that's real and getting worse—the problem is simpler and more mechanical. Billions of dollars in debt is maturing, and the math that made sense at 4.3% does not work at 6.2%. Banks are getting squeezed, borrowers are getting squeezed, and the reckoning is happening right now.
what_changed:
The Federal Reserve cut rates sharply from September 2024 through the end of 2025—a total of 1.75 percentage points—to ease pressure on banks and borrowers after the 2023 banking crisis took down SVB, Signature, and First Republic. But that relief was temporary and one-directional. The real problem sits in the debt that was issued years earlier, when rates were lower and office buildings still looked like safe bets. Between 2015 and 2022, commercial real estate borrowers locked in loans at rates around 4.3%. Now those loans are maturing. In 2025 alone, $957 billion in CRE loans came due for refinancing. Through 2028, $2.8 trillion more will mature. Today's rates for new CRE financing sit at 6.2%. The spread—190 basis points—is not a rounding error. For a $100 million office building loan, that's $1.9 million more per year in interest expense. Scale that to a portfolio or a whole asset class, and the math breaks.

The refinancing wave exposes a deeper structural problem. Office properties refinancing at 6.2% often cannot generate enough rental income to service the debt at the new rate. Commercial Mortgage-Backed Securities (CMBS) delinquencies hit 7.29% in 2025—the highest distress signal in years. Chapter 11 bankruptcies in the real estate sector hit a 10-year high in 2025, and corporate bankruptcies broadly reached 694 cases, the highest count in 14 years. The market knew this was coming, but knowing and absorbing it are different things. Banks are holding $2.7 trillion in CRE exposure on their balance sheets, concentrated in regional and community banks that lack the diversification of the mega-banks. When office tenancy fails and cap rates reset, the collateral value drops. A building worth $60 million based on rents six years ago might be worth $35 million based on what rents and interest rates say today. That gap is where losses live.

The Fed's rate cuts from mid-2024 into 2025 actually compressed banks' net interest margins even as they recovered slightly to 3.39% by Q4 2025—the highest since 2019—because deposit costs were sticky and slow to fall. Meanwhile, competition for deposits intensified. Uninsured deposits surged $214.7 billion in Q4 2025 alone, a sign that corporate clients and sophisticated investors were chasing yield and moving money to banks offering better rates. Banks needed higher yields on their loan books to offset deposit-cost pressure and compensate for credit losses on troubled CRE. But borrowers already stressed by rate resets cannot bear higher yields. The two sides are being crushed in the same vice: refinancing rates that destroy deal economics, and deposit competition that erodes the interest-rate cushion banks have left.

The real twist is that industrial and multifamily—the strongest real estate segments—are actually absorbing losses from office. Industrial had a banner 2025 with 940 million square feet of leasing, the second-best year on record, fueled by e-commerce tenants accounting for 56% of retail sales growth and needing 50 to 70 million square feet of warehouse space for every 1% rise in online penetration. Multifamily absorbed 124,600 units in Q2 2026 alone and drove 39.5% year-over-year growth in investor transaction volume, powered by a 3.4-million-unit housing shortage and a 105% premium to buy rather than rent. But both segments are refinancing into the same higher-rate environment. The difference is they earn enough to service the debt. Offices do not. This is creating a bifurcated market where strong asset classes are paying more to fund weak ones, and the debt wall is forcing a capital reallocation that looks less like recovery and more like triage.

Real estate investors with logistics and residential portfolios are consolidating and buying at distressed valuations from borrowers forced to sell. Banks lending to these strong segments are actually more profitable because yield is higher and credit losses are lower.
lose: Office building owners, especially those holding Class B and C properties, are getting crushed. The sector sits in structural crisis: office vacancy peaked at 19.6% in Q1 2025 and has only begun to decline as 127 million square feet was absorbed, but the underlying demand is gone. Refinancing that building at 6.2% often destroys the debt service coverage ratio. Owners are forced to refinance into the same higher-rate environment, accept losses on resale, or default. Community and regional banks holding concentrated CRE portfolios face margin compression from deposit competition and credit losses from office defaults. The $2.7 trillion in CRE exposure on bank balance sheets is not diversified enough in smaller banks to absorb losses on the weak segment while rates remain higher. Developers and building managers face obsolescence: office-to-apartment conversions reached 90,300 units in 2026, a 28% year-over-year jump, signaling a wholesale rewrite of the use case for millions of square feet that will never be profitable offices again.
worry: The single biggest risk is a cascading default spiral in office and secondary properties. When one major owner defaults on a $500 million or $1 billion property, it forces a mark-to-market loss on comparable collateral across the banking system, which triggers more defaults and more mark-downs in a feedback loop. The $2.7 trillion in CRE exposure sits concentrated in smaller banks that do not have the capital buffers or diversification to absorb a 10% or 20% loss on their portfolio. A wave of bank failures in 2026 or 2027, timed to coincide with the peak refinancing wall, could trigger a credit crunch that starves even strong borrowers (industrial, multifamily) of capital to expand or refinance. The broader economy would suffer not because the real estate problem is new, but because the debt maturity cliff is concentrated in time and overlaps with rising labor costs and energy prices.

title: Building Costs Bite
dek: Tariffs, labor, and rates raise the cost to build anything new.
lede: The construction industry is caught in a vise. Labor shortages, tariff shocks, and elevated borrowing costs have made new buildings more expensive to build and harder to finance. The split is brutal: data centers (the only growth story) are surging while traditional offices, retail, and housing are stalling.
what_changed:
The commercial construction market in the US is $315.5 billion in 2026, growing just 1.1%—a reflection of a deep, two-tier split. Data center construction is the only engine: starts reached $77.7 billion in 2025, a stunning 190% jump from 2024, as Amazon commits $23 billion to an Ohio facility and Microsoft deploys what it calls the world's most powerful data center in Wisconsin, both coming online in 2026. The Stargate Project, a $500 billion four-year AI infrastructure investment by OpenAI, SoftBank, Oracle, and MGX announced in January 2025, anchors long-term pipelines. But office construction hit a wall. Hybrid work hollowed out office demand by 41% since 2019; new office deliveries dropped 26% in 2025, and vacancy concentrates in older Class-B and Class-C towers while Class-A trophy buildings stay full at premium rents. Retail, warehouse, and hospitality remain soft but stable—no recovery in sight.

The binding constraint is labor scarcity, which now costs the industry $10.8 billion annually. A 500,000-worker shortage has pushed wage inflation to 4% per year and forced mid-market contractors to turn away work. Material costs are surging from tariff shocks: effective tariff rates on construction goods hit 25–30% in 2025 (the highest in 40 years), raising the typical home cost by $10,900 per unit. December 2025 saw monthly spending on data center construction average $6.5 billion—up from just $500 million in mid-2021. Elevated mortgage rates at 5.7–6.6% in August 2026 have frozen financing for traditional commercial deals, squeezing both developers and lenders.

The home builders industry reflects this pain even more sharply. At $166.2 billion in 2026, the market is flat (0.0% growth in 2026, 1.1% CAGR from 2021–2026) and margins are compressed to 6–8% net, down from 6.1% in 2022. Housing starts crashed 15.4% month-over-month in May 2026 to 1.177 million (seasonally adjusted annual rate), the lowest since May 2020, as buyers confronted the combined shock of tariff-driven costs and persistent high rates near 6%. Builders have cut prices by an average of 5% and are offering mortgage rate buydowns to move inventory, hollowing out profits. Sixty percent of builders report tariff-driven cost increases; smaller builders are hit hardest because they cannot absorb the margin squeeze. M&A activity among home builders doubled between August 2025 and June 2026: 18% of builders report acquisition approaches (up from 9%), signaling that scale and capital strength now separate winners from sellers. Major deals include Taylor Morrison acquired by Berkshire Hathaway, Tri Pointe Homes acquired by Sumitomo Forestry, and United Homes Group and Holiday Builders acquired by Stanley Martin Homes. Construction M&A deals as a whole surged 18.2% to 562 transactions in 2025 as firms consolidated to offset labor shortages and rising input costs.

This is a structural reckoning, not a cycle. Tariff regimes are sticky, labor shortages reflect demographic collapse, and rates will not reset to 3% overnight. The data center boom is real and capital-intensive, but it does not employ construction workers at the same scale as mid-market office and retail projects. Smaller builders, independent contractors, and traditional commercial developers face a narrowing window: either consolidate, pivot to niche markets (or niche markets), or exit.

title: The Real-Estate Reckoning
dek: Hybrid work and higher rates have shattered the old real-estate math; capital now rotates away from offices toward logistics, data centers, and housing.
lede: The math broke in two directions at once. Hybrid work hollowed out downtown offices—office vacancy peaked at 19.6% in Q1 2025 and only fell to 17.7% by mid-2026 after 127 million square feet of absorption, revealing that Class B and C office buildings are now economically obsolete. At the same time, interest-rate hikes destroyed the leverage game that built modern real estate: $957 billion in commercial real estate loans matured in 2025 alone, with another $2.8 trillion due through 2028, and refinancing at higher rates is simply unaffordable. Capital that once chased office towers and debt-fueled deals now hunts for hard assets with real cash flow: warehouses for e-commerce, data centers for AI compute, and housing stock for a shortage that sits at 3.4 million homes.
what_changed:
The office sector entered structural crisis. National office vacancy climbed steadily, then got stuck at an artificially low 17.7% by mid-2026 only because developers were forced to accept conversions to apartments—90,300 office-to-apartment conversion units in 2026 alone, a 28% year-over-year jump, now representing 47% of the entire 193,900-unit adaptive reuse pipeline. The tenants willing to stay in class A trophy assets in major CBDs paid premium rates, but everyone else either left or never showed up. Class B and C buildings became insolvent: landlords couldn't raise rents, refinancing windows slammed shut, and Chapter 11 bankruptcies among commercial real estate owners hit a 10-year high in 2025 with 694 corporate bankruptcies (the highest in 14 years). CMBS delinquencies reached 7.29% in 2025, the highest distress signal in the market, and multifamily loan delinquencies hit 1.37% in Q3 2025—a 3.4× increase over two years and the worst level since 2008.

Industrial real estate and data centers captured all the growth. Logistics operators leased 940 million square feet in 2025, the second-best year on record, driven by e-commerce tenants accounting for 56% of retail goods sales growth and requiring 50-70 million square feet of warehouse space for every 1% increase in online share. Colocation facilities for AI exploded: the US market jumped from $46.84 billion in 2025 to $72.37 billion in 2026, a 55% spike in one year, with growth driven by AI infrastructure demand—training workloads burning 30-100+ kW per rack, inference pulling 10-20 kW, all requiring liquid cooling and direct power ties. North American colocation occupancy hit 1% vacancy by 2026 (nearly full), forcing operators to treat power access and regulatory tariffs as the new competitive moats rather than square footage. Grid interconnection queues now exceed 1,400 GW of stuck requests with four-to-five-year lead times in saturated markets like Northern Virginia, Dallas, and Phoenix. Federal regulators issued data-center-specific transmission tariffs in December 2025, and states rushed their own: Oregon's POWER Act (August 2025) mandated 10-year power-purchase agreements for facilities larger than 20 MW.

Multifamily housing absorbed capital and buyers because the shortage is real. Apartment rents stopped climbing in 2025-2026 after years of double-digit growth, with luxury vacancy jumping to 11.4%, but the underlying squeeze remains: 3.4 million homes short, and buying costs 105% more than renting on an equivalent basis. Multifamily net absorption hit 124,600 units in Q2 2026, and investor transaction volume surged 39.5% year-over-year, signaling capital rotating into housing despite modest rental growth forecasted at 1.2% for 2026. The apartment market is consolidating at brutal scale: AvalonBay Communities and Equity Residential announced a $69 billion merger in late 2025 (closing in 2026) to create the nation's largest apartment REIT with 180,000+ units and expected $175 million in cost cuts within 18 months. Pinnacle filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in May 2025 over $500 million in mortgage debt, and its 5,100 rent-stabilized NYC apartments were auctioned off. Sonder Holdings, the coliving platform, filed for Chapter 7 liquidation in 2025 after its Marriott licensing deal collapsed due to poor financial performance. Smaller multifamily operators and leveraged owners are bleeding out.

Home builders are trapped in a flat, high-friction equilibrium where tariffs and elevated rates have compressed margins while consolidating power to the top tier. Tariffs on construction goods hit 25-30% effective rates by 2025—the highest in 40 years—adding $10,900 per home on average, while skilled labor shortages cost the industry $10.8 billion annually with 4% annual wage growth. Builders responded by cutting prices 5% and offering mortgage rate buydowns, hollowing out margins to 6-8% net in 2026. Housing starts crashed 15.4% month-over-month to 1.177 million annualized by May 2026 (the lowest since May 2020) as buyers faced combined shocks of tariff-driven costs and rates stuck near 6%. M&A activity among builders doubled between August 2025 and June 2026; 18% of builders reported acquisition approaches, up from 9% in August 2025, with major deals like Taylor Morrison acquired by Berkshire Hathaway, Tri Pointe Homes acquired by Sumitomo Forestry, and United Homes Group acquired by Stanley Martin Homes signaling that capital strength and scale now separate winners from sellers. Smaller builders lack the balance sheets to absorb tariff shocks or the refinancing capacity to survive rate cycles.
